name: Paul Volcker

summary.text: Paul A. Volcker was Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board from August 6, 1979 until August 11, 1987. In 1980, after the collapse of the silver price, the Hunt brothers' Placid Oil negotiated a bank loan of about $1.1 billion; Volcker testified that he neither initiated nor guided the loan negotiations, while TIME reported that his monitoring of the talks was read by bankers as Fed approval of a bailout despite the Fed's credit-restraint program, and he said the Hunts would have to sell much of their silver to qualify. In August 1982, when Mexico said it could not keep servicing its debt, the Fed convened central bankers to arrange a bridge loan and encouraged U.S. banks to reschedule Mexico's loans; Volcker later cited the Latin American debt problem as a factor in the Fed's July 1982 decision to ease policy.

sources.title: Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s

facts.claim: Volcker became Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board on August 6, 1979, was reappointed in 1983, and served until August 11, 1987.
facts.quote: He became chairman on August 6, 1979, was reappointed in 1983, and served until August 11, 1987.

facts.claim: TIME reported in 1980 that Placid Oil, the Dallas oil company owned by Bunker and Herbert Hunt and four Hunt children, was negotiating a nine-year $1.1 billion loan after the silver collapse, and that Volcker testified he neither initiated nor guided the loan negotiations, although his continual monitoring was interpreted by bankers to mean the Fed, despite its credit-restraint policy, favored some kind of bailout.
facts.quote: Volcker testified last week that he neither initiated nor guided the negotiations for any loans to the Hunts, his continual monitoring of the situation was interpreted by bankers to mean that the Federal Reserve, despite its credit restraint policy, favored some kind of bailout

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported in April 1980 that Volcker said the Hunt brothers would have to sell much of their silver holdings to qualify for $1 billion in bank loans, and in May 1980 that a Fed report indicated almost two-thirds of the $1 billion would go to pay the Hunts' debts to foreign banks or obligations of an offshore silver investment company.
facts.quote: almost two-thirds of the $1 billion will be used either to pay the Hunts debts to foreign banks or to meet obligations of an offshore silver investment company

sources.title: Hunt Loans Will Settle Debt Abroad

facts.claim: UPI reported in 1985 that under the arrangement with the Fed the Hunts were required to dispose of their silver by 1990, and described the 1980 bank loans as a $1.1 billion bailout orchestrated by Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker.
facts.quote: under the arrangement with the Fed, the Hunts were required to dispose of their silver by 1990

sources.title: Business World: The Hunts 'America's wealthiest family struggles to keep image, empire'

facts.claim: In August 1982 Mexico's finance minister told the Fed chairman, the Treasury secretary and the IMF managing director that Mexico could not keep servicing its roughly $80 billion debt; the Fed convened an emergency meeting of central bankers to provide a bridge loan to Mexico and encouraged U.S. banks to participate in rescheduling Mexico's loans.
facts.quote: In August, the Fed convened an emergency meeting of central bankers from around the world to provide a bridge loan to Mexico. Fed officials also encouraged US banks to participate in a program to reschedule Mexico's loans.

sources.title: Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s

facts.claim: Volcker said the strains of 1982, including the prospective Mexican crisis and the Penn Square bankruptcy, contributed to the timing of the Fed's decision to ease policy in July 1982, ending the tightening cycle.
facts.quote: All this contributed to the timing of our decision to ease policy in July 1982

sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Review
sources.title: The Volcker Tightening Cycle: Explaining the 1982 Course Reversal

facts.claim: Federal Reserve History states that during his second term Volcker monitored the debt crisis in developing countries and supported expansion of the IMF's reserve fund, and that these events dominated much of his focus as Chairman.
facts.quote: Volcker monitored the debt crisis in developing countries and supported the expansion of the International Monetary Fund's reserve fund.

connections.claim: Volcker chaired the Federal Reserve Board from August 1979 to August 1987.
connections.quote: He became chairman on August 6, 1979, was reappointed in 1983, and served until August 11, 1987.

connections.claim: In 1980 Volcker monitored, and testified about, the bank loan negotiations for the Hunts' Placid Oil after the silver collapse; he said the Hunts would have to sell much of their silver to qualify.
connections.quote: Volcker testified last week that he neither initiated nor guided the negotiations for any loans to the Hunts

connections.claim: Volcker supported the expansion of the IMF's reserve fund during the 1980s developing-country debt crisis.
connections.quote: supported the expansion of the International Monetary Fund's reserve fund

openQuestions: Site claim that Volcker's Fed 'did not block the $1.1 billion bank loan to the Hunts' Placid Oil despite its credit-restraint program': broadly supported by TIME and UPI, with the caveat that Volcker testified he neither initiated nor guided the negotiations and sources give the loan as $1 billion to $1.1 billion.

Site claim that Volcker 'managed the rolling sovereign debt reschedulings to protect US banks': Federal Reserve History confirms the Fed convened a bridge loan for Mexico and encouraged banks to reschedule; the stated motive of protecting U.S. banks is not in the sources returned.
The 1988 civil conspiracy verdict against the Hunts and the exchange rule changes of January 1980 were not researched here.
